chapter_theme: Opens the Renunciation sarukkam: King Payapati, delighting in his grandchildren, thinks that his kingship is the fruit of past good deeds and the body is foul and brief, then asks his ministers whether any statecraft can defeat Death; they cannot, and a minister proposes seeking the sages.

cast.role: King Payapati of Podanam, called Prajapati in 1841, who turns to renunciation
Tivittan, the red-eyed lord, the king's son
the king's grandchildren, the young sons of the discus-ruler

1840.reading: The poet opens the Renunciation sarukkam: while Payapati, king of kings, sat happily listening to the sweet babble of his son's children, he entered true renunciation, and the poet will tell how.
1840.nuance: The turn is set in a moment of family joy, not of loss: the call to renounce comes with the grandchildren's laughter in the room, so the sarukkam begins from fullness, not grief.
1840.event: The poet announces that King Payapati took to renunciation while delighting in his grandchildren.

1841.reading: As the red-eyed lord bows, King Prajapati sits glad among his own, and the grandchildren, their ornaments ringing, run up to the ruler of the discus.
1841.nuance: Payapati and Prajapati name the same king of Podanam in these verses; the red-eyed bowing lord and the 'ruler of the discus' are taken as Tivittan on the strength of the earlier chapters, and the children as his sons.
1841.event: Tivittan bows to Prajapati, and Tivittan's young sons run to their grandfather.

1842.reading: Seeing the children's nectar-sweet smiles, the king says that the swollen merit which has brought such pleasure still has more seed to be sown.
1842.nuance: The pleasure is read as a harvest already drawn from a field, so the same sight that delights him prompts the thought of sowing; the verse does not say the pleasure is bad, only that the stock behind it is finite.
1842.event: Payapati, watching his grandchildren, speaks of sowing more seed for the austerity that bore these pleasures.

claims.claim: pleasures enjoyed now are the fruit of earlier austerity, and more must be sown for the future

1843.reading: The umbrellas, the kings who surround him, the world's bowing and the ride on a tall elephant are all a gift to us from our good-deed deity.
1843.nuance: நல்வினைத் தெய்வம் makes karma itself the divinity who grants the kingship; no god of the Veda is named. The king receives what he has earned.

claims.claim: royal honour is given by one's own good deeds as by a deity

1844.reading: Those who try to destroy the root of the good deed that made them king and gave them the sea-girt earth, the only helper that goes with the life, are base men and will be kings in the hells.
1844.nuance: நரகங்கட்கு அரசர் turns kingship upside down: the same word that names his rank names the hell-lord's dominion for the heedless.

claims.claim: one who spends the stock of good deeds without renewing it falls to hell
the good deed is the one benefactor that accompanies the life

1845.reading: Whether the days gone by pass and wealth and pride stand, one need not suffer on the path; we live as today, but if the day of our perishing comes our life is worth nothing.
1845.nuance: The verse is hard to construe in lines 1-2; the reading takes it as the king's inward objection that he is content as things are, answered at once by line 4.

claims.claim: life lived on pleasure alone has no worth once death comes

1846.reading: Two days make a bright young leaf green, then pale, then a dried leaf that falls and burns to dust; the ignorant who see it and still say 'we will live' cannot be held back.
1846.nuance: The leaf stands for the body in three stages, flame-red, emerald and withered, so the argument from nature rests on colour change, not only on loss.

claims.claim: youth and life wither as a leaf does, yet the unwise ignore it

1847.reading: People are born, grow great, then die, and no one has lived on hidden; so, heart, think that nothing is better than austerity.
1847.nuance: The king addresses his own heart (நெஞ்சே); the same address runs through 1848 and 1849.

claims.claim: everyone born dies, and austerity is the best answer

1848.reading: The foolish body we tend is as good as dead; if we leave attachment and stop clinging, who is better than we; think this over, he told his heart.
1848.nuance: Lines 1-2 are hard to construe and the reading is tentative; line 3 and 4 are clearer.

claims.claim: letting go of attachment is the mark of the best

1849.reading: The body wreathed, perfumed and smoked for display falls apart and runs with filth when a tiny thorn from the hair pricks it, yet we are glad of it without shame, heart.
1849.nuance: The adornment is listed step by step (garland, paste, incense) before the thorn undoes it, which makes the care itself the evidence of folly.

claims.claim: the adorned body is a foul thing and no cause for pride

1850.reading: The foul flowing fluid of this body, which the demon spirits would mock if it were turned inside out, would be fought over by kites and crows, who are kept off with a stick, and so do a thousand kinds of 'beauty' circle it.
1850.nuance: The crow guarded off with a hand stick (line 3) is the very picture Naladiyar 41 uses; the shared image makes the point that the body must be defended from what will eat it. Line 4 is hard to construe.

claims.claim: the body is foul within and beauty is only an outer cover

1851.reading: Those who did evil deeds take its seed and sow it; like a man in a tiger's mouth, they leave the root of good deeds that feeds them sweetly and die wanting the pleasure of what has no root, which fools do.
1851.nuance: The verse repeats 1844's root image in the plain voice of a warning and ends the king's inward reflection before 1852 opens the council.

claims.claim: those who abandon the root of good deeds for fleeting pleasure perish

1852.reading: Having reflected on all this and judged that waiting is excess, the king summons his counsellors through his attendants and, seated with his ministers in the coral-pillared gem hall, speaks.
1852.event: Payapati calls his ministers to a council in the gem hall.

1853.reading: The king asks the ministers to tell what losses may come to his enduring wealth, which kings cannot seize like a mountain elephant nor thieves steal like women's glances.
1853.nuance: The wealth is described by what cannot take it (kings, thieves), which prepares the answer that only Death remains.
1853.event: Payapati asks the council to name any danger to his wealth.

1854.reading: The ministers answer that, with effort and good order guarding the realm, no theft or force can reach it; is anything more to come, they ask, unless the ranging Death should come near?
1854.nuance: The ministers name the one danger they cannot guard against, so the council turns by their own words from the state to Death.
1854.event: The ministers reply that nothing threatens the realm but Death.

claims.claim: a king's wealth is safe from kings and thieves but not from Death

1855.reading: At the king's bidding to speak from learning about what Death can take, the ministers, reading his mind, say that Death will do his day's work and take their lives whole.
1855.event: At the king's bidding, the ministers say Death will take their lives.

claims.claim: death comes on its day and takes life whole

1856.reading: The king asks whether Death can be turned back by conciliation, by alliance, by making enemies first, or by attacking and conquering him, and bids them name a way to live.
1856.nuance: The questions are the four ordinary expedients of a ruler against an enemy; the king tests whether statecraft reaches Death.
1856.event: Payapati asks the ministers if statecraft can defeat Death.

1857.reading: The ministers answer that they have not learned a stratagem to leap at the king of Death, who spreads sickness, takes lives by force and eats them.
1857.event: The ministers confess that statecraft has no means against Death.

1858.reading: Then, says the king, the pleasures of royal wealth we enjoy and the life we wish to live are like a fawn grazing the green weed while the tiger prepares to spring.
1858.nuance: The simile is the king's answer to the council's silence; it turns their confession into his own resolve.

claims.claim: life lived in pleasure is a fawn grazing before the tiger springs

1859.reading: The speaker answers that there is not even that much time: like a morsel falling into a rutting elephant's mouth, Death, glad with his crescent tooth, takes life in the space of a blink.
1859.nuance: The speaker is not named; he addresses the king as வேந்தே, so a minister is meant.

claims.claim: the interval before death is shorter than a blink

1860.reading: The king, who loses his life, says that flatterers who cannot serve the lord's interest with sweet words cannot help; look to the learned who advise him, and tell of some refuge we can reach beyond Death.
1860.nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe; the verse is read as the king rejecting courtly flattery and asking for refuge.
1860.event: Payapati asks what refuge lies beyond Death.

1861.reading: Dismissing the pleasant flattery that ends only in ruin, the speaker, taking the king's thought to heart, asks, lord, whether they should try after bowing to the sages and hearing them.
1861.nuance: கண்ணனார் is taken as the speaker's own epithet in line 2; the verse is uncertain in lines 2-3.
1861.event: A minister proposes to seek the sages' counsel.

1862.reading: Lord of fertile lands, there is no refuge but to stay at the foot of the austere sage's feet, close under the tree of his refuge; what other refuge can there be?
1862.nuance: The refuge is a person, the sage under his tree, not a god or a rite; the verse sets the sage's feet against the king's palace as a shelter.

claims.claim: the feet of the austere sage are the only refuge against death

links.note: 1842 says more seed must be sown for the austerity that bore present pleasure; 1851 shows those who instead cut the root and die.
links.teaches: The warning of 1851 is the unsown field that 1842 fears, so the king's wish to sow is shown as the way out of that ruin.

links.note: 1843 reads the kingship and the bowing kings as the gift of the good-deed deity; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants under umbrellas fall when deeds turn.
links.teaches: Read together, the umbrellas that 1843 credits to past merit are the same ones Naladiyar says a turn of deeds can remove.

gains.a: The grant of kingship gains an explicit reversal: what a good deed gave, a turn of deeds can take back.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an account of why the king rose, through the good-deed god, which it assumes without saying.

links.note: 1844 calls those who destroy the root of good deeds base; 1851 shows them leaving the root that feeds them sweetly.
links.teaches: The root of good deeds is a recurring image whose repetition shows the king returning to the same fear from two sides.

links.note: 1847 concludes that nothing is better than austerity; Kural 46 asks what is gained by going the outside way if household life is lived in virtue.
links.teaches: The pair turns on whether household virtue is enough: the king answers from the certainty of death, the couplet from the sufficiency of aram.

gains.a: The king's resolve gains the opposing case that a householder who keeps aram may need no leaving.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler for whom death makes household virtue seem insufficient.

links.note: 1849 shows the adorned body undone by one small prick; Naladiyar 41 says a bit of skin torn off needs a stick to drive away crows.
links.teaches: Both break the body's finery with a trivial injury, but the epic does it for a king examining his own display, the quatrain to answer a lover's praise.

gains.a: The king's reflection gains the quatrain's crows, which the injury will draw.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a body decked with garland, paste and incense that the injury undoes.

links.note: 1850 has crows and kites guarded off with a hand stick; Naladiyar 41 has the stick that drives the crows from the torn body.
links.teaches: The same stick appears for two different speakers, a king guarding himself and a poet mocking the lover, which shows how fixed the picture was.

gains.a: The verse gains a second use of the stick and the crow, as a rebuke of those who call the body lovely.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king speaking of his own body in the same terms.

links.note: 1850 turns on the body's filth to set aside kingly pride; Thiruppugazh 146 describes the same filth as a house of diseases and asks Murugan for grace.
links.teaches: The Jain king ends his disgust in a plan to leave and seek sages, while the Thiruppugazh ends the same disgust in a plea for a god's feet.

gains.a: The verse gains a different exit from the body's foulness, a god's grace in place of the sage's feet.
gains.b: The poem gains a king who draws the opposite practical conclusion from the same catalogue.

links.note: 1856 tests whether any statecraft can escape Death; Naladiyar 6 says none here has leapt clear and bids the wealthy give.
links.teaches: The king tries the four expedients the quatrain never names, and by their failure the quatrain's rule is shown by a ruler's own attempt.

gains.a: The question gains the rule that no one leapt clear, so the ministers' failure is not their own.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a ruler who actually tries every device of power to escape.

links.note: 1859 shortens the term to a blink before Death; Kural 334 calls the day a blade that saws the life.
links.teaches: The epic shortens the quantity: the couplet measures life as days, the verse measures it by the blink the minister names.

gains.a: The blink gains the blade as an image for time's cutting.
gains.b: The couplet gains a minister who counts the cut in a blink.

links.note: 1860 asks for a refuge beyond Death; 1862 answers that none exists but the austere sage's feet.
links.teaches: The question and the answer divide the council's work: the king asks, the minister names the sage's feet.

links.note: 1862 names the austere sage's feet as the only refuge from Death; Tirumanthiram 2 praises Siva who kicked Death and became king of the south.
links.teaches: The two refuges differ in kind: a teacher's feet to be reached by one's own austerity, against a god who defeated Death himself.

gains.a: The sage's feet gain a rival refuge in a god who has already defeated Death.
gains.b: The invocation gains a Jain-framed answer that makes the sage, not Siva, the shelter.

source_issues: Verses 1840-1855 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1842 line 5 and 1849 line 6 carried a pulli after a vowel sign, repaired by the build.
1848 and 1850 are hard to construe; 1860 to 1862 turn on rare words and the speaker of 1859 and 1861 is not named; the readings are marked uncertain.
